{{short description|Formula for number of orbits of a group action}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2020}}
'''Burnside's lemma''', sometimes also called '''Burnside's counting theorem''', the '''Cauchy–Frobenius lemma''', or the '''orbit-counting theorem''', is a result in [[group theory]] that is often useful in taking account of [[symmetry]] when counting mathematical objects. It was discovered by [[Augustin Louis Cauchy]] and [[Ferdinand Georg Frobenius]], and became well known after [[William Burnside]] quoted it.<ref>{{harvnb|Burnside|1897|loc=§119}}</ref> The result [[Enumerative combinatorics|enumerates]] orbits of a symmetry group acting on some objects: that is, it counts distinct objects, considering objects symmetric to each other as the same; or counting distinct objects [[up to]] a symmetry [[equivalence relation]]; or counting only objects in [[canonical form]]. For example, in describing possible organic compounds of certain type, one considers them up to spatial rotation symmetry: different rotated drawings of a given molecule are chemically identical (whereas a mirror reflection might give a [[Chirality|different compound]]).

== Statement ==
Let <math>G</math> be a [[finite set|finite]] [[group (mathematics)|group]] that [[Group action (mathematics)|acts]] on a [[Set (mathematics)|set]] <math>X</math>. For each <math>g</math> in <math>G</math>, let <math>X^g</math> denote the set of [[element (mathematics)|element]]s in <math>X</math> that are [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed by]] <math>g</math> (left [[invariant (mathematics)|invariant]] by <math>g</math>): that is, <math>X^g = \{ x \in X : g\cdot x = x\}.</math>  Burnside's lemma asserts the following formula for the number of [[orbit (group theory)|orbit]]s, denoted <math>|X/G|</math>:<ref>{{harvnb|Rotman|1995|loc=Chapter 3}}</ref>

<math display="block">|X/G| = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g \in G}|X^g|.</math>

Thus the number of orbits (a [[natural number]] or [[infinity|+∞]]) is equal to the [[average]] number of points fixed by an element of ''G''. For an infinite group <math>G</math>, there is still a [[bijection]]:

<math display="block">G \times X/G \ \longleftrightarrow\ \coprod_{g \in G} X^g . </math>

== Examples ==
===Necklaces===
There are 8 possible [[bit vector|bit string]]s of length 3, but tying together the string ends gives only four distinct 2-colored [[Necklace (combinatorics)|necklaces]] of length 3, given by the canonical forms 000, 001, 011, 111: the other strings 100 and 010 are equivalent to 001 by rotation, while 110 and 101 are equivalent to 011.  That is, rotation equivalence [[partition of a set|partitions]] the set <math>X</math> of strings into four [[equivalence class]]s, aka orbits: <math display="block">X = \{{000}\}\cup \{{001}, {010}, {100}\}\cup \{{011}, {101}, {110}\}\cup \{{111}\}.</math>The Burnside formula uses the number of rotations, which is 3 including the null rotation, and the number of bit strings left unchanged by each rotation. All eight bit strings are unchanged by the null rotation, and two (000 and 111) are unchanged by the other two rotations. Thus the number of orbits is:
<math display="block">4 = \frac{1}{3}(8+2+2).</math>

For length 4, there are 16 possible bit strings; 4 rotations; the null rotation leaves all 16 strings unchanged; the 1-rotation and 3-rotation each leave two strings unchanged (0000 and 1111); the 2-rotation leaves 4 bit strings unchanged (0000, 0101, 1010, 1111). The number of distinct necklaces is thus: <math>6 = \tfrac{1}{4}(16+2+4+2)</math>, represented by the canonical forms 0000, 0001, 0011, 0101, 0111, 1111.

The general case of ''n'' bits and ''k'' colors is given by a [[necklace polynomial]].

=== Colorings of a cube ===
Burnside's lemma can compute the number of rotationally distinct colourings of the faces of a [[Cube (geometry)|cube]] using three colours.

Let <math>X</math> be the set of 3<sup>6</sup> possible face color combinations that can be applied to a fixed cube, and let the rotation group ''G'' of the cube act on <math>X</math> by moving the colored faces: two colorings in <math>X</math> belong to the same orbit precisely when one is a rotation of the other. Rotationally distinct colorings correspond to group orbits, and can be found by counting the sizes of the [[fixed set]]s for the 24 elements of ''G'', the colorings left unchanged by each rotation:

[[File:Face colored cube.png|thumb|Cube with coloured faces]]
* the [[identity element]] fixes all 3<sup>6</sup> colorings
* six 90-degree face rotations each fix 3<sup>3</sup> colorings
* three 180-degree face rotations each fix 3<sup>4</sup> colorings
* eight 120-degree vertex rotations each fix 3<sup>2</sup> colorings
* six 180-degree edge rotations each fix 3<sup>3</sup> colorings.

A detailed examination may be found
[[Cycle index#The cycle index of the face permutations of a cube|here]].

The average fixed-set size is thus:

: <math> |X/G| = \frac{1}{24}\left(3^6+6\cdot 3^3 + 3 \cdot 3^4 + 8 \cdot 3^2 + 6 \cdot 3^3 \right) = 57. </math>

There are 57 rotationally distinct colourings of the faces of a cube in three colours. In general, the number of rotationally distinct colorings of the faces of a cube in ''n'' colors is:

: <math> \frac{1}{24}\left(n^6+3n^4 + 12n^3 + 8n^2\right). </math>

=== Conjugacy classes ===
Let <math> G </math> be a finite group. Consider the group action of <math> G </math> on itself given by the [[conjugation (group theory)|conjugation]] map <math> g \mapsto \phi_g </math> where <math> \phi_g(h) = g h g^{-1} </math>. The orbits are the [[conjugacy class]]es of <math> G </math> and the set of fixed points of an element <math> g </math> is the [[centralizer]] <math> C_G(g) </math>. Thus, by Burnside's lemma, the number of conjugacy classes of <math>G</math> is equal to <math>\frac{1}{|G|} \sum_g |C_G(g)|</math>, that is, the average size of the centralizer.

== Proof ==

In the proof of Burnside's lemma, the first step is to re-express the sum over the group elements ''g''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''G'' as an equivalent sum over the set of elements ''x''&nbsp;∈&nbsp;''X'':

:<math>\sum_{g \in G}|X^g| = \#\{(g,x)\in G\times X \mid g \cdot x = x\} = \sum_{x \in X} |G_x|.</math>

Here <math>X^g = \{ x \in X : g\cdot x = x\}</math> is the set of points of <math>X</math> fixed by the element <math>g</math> of <math>G</math>, whereas <math>G_x = \{ g \in G : g\cdot x = x\}</math> is the [[stabilizer subgroup]] of <math>G</math>, consisting of those symmetries that fix the point <math>x \in X</math>.

The [[orbit-stabilizer theorem]] says that for each <math>x \in X</math> there is a natural [[bijection]] between the orbit <math>G \cdot x = \{ g\cdot x : g \in G\}</math> and the set of left cosets <math>G / G_x</math>.  [[Lagrange's theorem (group theory)|Lagrange's theorem]] implies that

<math display="block">|G \cdot x| = [G : G_x] = |G| / |G_x|.</math>

The sum may therefore be rewritten as

<math display="block">\sum_{x \in X} |G_x| = \sum_{x \in X} \frac{|G|}{|G \cdot x|} = |G| \sum_{x \in X}\frac{1}{|G \cdot x|}.</math>

Writing <math>X</math> as the [[disjoint union]] of its orbits in <math>X/G</math> gives

<math display="block">|G| \sum_{x \in X}\frac{1}{|G \cdot x|}  
 = |G| \sum_{A\in X/G} \sum_{x\in A} \frac{1}{|A|}  
 = |G| \sum_{A\in X/G} 1  =  |G|\cdot|X/G|. </math>

Putting everything together gives the desired result:

<math display="block">\sum_{g \in G}|X^g| = |G| \cdot |X/G|.</math>

This is similar to the proof of the [[class equation|conjugacy class equation]], which considers the conjugation action of <math>G</math> on itself, that is, it is the case <math>X = G</math> and <math>g \cdot x = gxg^{-1}</math>, so that the stabilizer of <math>x</math> is the centralizer <math>G_x = Z_G(x)</math>.

==Enumeration vs. generation==
Burnside's lemma counts distinct objects, but it does not construct them. In general, combinatorial generation with isomorph rejection considers the symmetries of <math>g</math> on objects <math>x</math>. But instead of checking that <math>g \cdot x = x</math>, it checks that <math>g \cdot x</math> has not already been generated.  One way to accomplish this is by checking that <math>g \cdot x</math> is not lexicographically less than <math>x</math>, using the lexicographically least member of each equivalence class as the canonical form of the class.<ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1145/187387.187400 | title=Isomorphism and the N-Queens problem | year=1994 | last1=Cull | first1=Paul | last2=Pandey | first2=Rajeev | journal=ACM SIGCSE Bulletin | volume=26 | issue=3 | pages=29–36 | s2cid=207183291 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Counting the objects generated with such a technique can verify that Burnside's lemma was correctly applied.

==History: the lemma that is not Burnside's==
[[William Burnside]] stated and proved this lemma in his 1897 book on finite groups, attributing it to {{harvnb|Frobenius|1887}}. But even prior to Frobenius, the formula was known to [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]] in 1845. Consequently, this lemma is sometimes referred to as the '''lemma that is not Burnside's'''.<ref>{{Cite journal | last1=Neumann | first1=Peter M. | author1-link=Peter M. Neumann | title=A lemma that is not Burnside's | mr=562002 | year=1979 | journal=The Mathematical Scientist | issn=0312-3685 | volume=4 | issue=2 | pages=133–141}}.</ref> The attribution of the lemma to someone other than its original discoverer is an example of [[Stigler's law of eponymy]].
